banana: A peel takes two years to break down in a landfill but only weeks in a compost pile. Oxygen makes all the difference.
apple: An apple core is 84% water and vanishes in a compost pile in about two months. Sealed in a landfill, it just sits there.
eggshells: Crushed shells add calcium to compost, and gardeners swear they deter slugs. The slugs have not confirmed this.
coffee-grounds: Grounds are nitrogen-rich "greens" in composting terms, and worms love them. Your earthworms are basically tiny baristas.
leaves: Shredded leaves are considered the gold standard of compost browns. One mature tree drops thousands every fall.
newspaper: One of the most recycled materials on earth. Newsprint can be reborn up to 7 times before the fibers give out.
cardboard-box: The average box is already about 50% recycled fiber. Boxes are the overachievers of the bin world.
glass-jar: Glass recycles forever with zero quality loss. A jar you recycle today could have been a jar in ancient Rome, in spirit.
alu-can: Recycling a can saves 95% of the energy of making one from bauxite, and it can be back on a shelf in 60 days.
office-paper: A sheet of office paper can be recycled 5 to 7 times. The fibers just get shorter and more tired each round, like the rest of us.
tin-can: "Tin" cans are actually steel with a whisper of tin, and steel is the most recycled material in the world by weight.
foam-cup: Foam is 95% air, which is why it's terrible to recycle — you're mostly shipping air to a facility that doesn't want it.
chip-bag: Chip bags are metallized film fused in layers no sorter can separate. Dark inside so chips stay fresh, shiny outside so you buy them.
cig-butt: Butts are the most littered item on earth, trillions a year, and the filter is plastic, not cotton. It'll outlive the smoker.
cig-butts: Same story in triplicate: cellulose acetate filters that take a decade to break down, leaching nicotine the whole way.
broken-pen: A ballpoint holds about five different plastics and metals. Separating them costs more than the pen ever did.
bottle: The plastic bottle was patented in 1973, and nearly every one ever made still exists somewhere — unless it became a fleece jacket.
bottle-red: Colored plastic is harder to recycle than clear because the dye limits what it can become next. Clear bottles have the brightest future.
pizza-box: Oil breaks paper fibers' bond so a greasy box can't be recycled — but compost microbes don't care about grease at all.
yard-debris: Yard waste rotting in a landfill makes methane. Composted, the same pile becomes soil instead of greenhouse gas.
corn-husks: Pure compost gold: they break down fast and add structure. A corn-heavy pile is basically a campfire that never lights.
bouquet: Flowers compost fine, but bouquets hide plastic water tubes and rubber bands. Florists sneak in more plastic than you'd think.
coffee-filter: Toss filter, grounds and all — it's all compostable. The rare case where the lazy option is the right one.
napkin: Napkin fibers are too short and food-soiled to recycle, but those same short fibers break down beautifully in compost.
chopsticks: Tens of billions of disposable chopsticks are used yearly. Untreated wood composts in weeks; lacquered ones belong in the trash.
sixpack-carrier: Rings take centuries to break down and famously entangle wildlife. Snipping them before tossing is a genuine kindness.
junk-mail: The average household gets 800+ pieces a year. It's all recyclable paper, plastic envelope windows included.
yogurt-tub: Tubs are #5 polypropylene, which fewer programs take than #1 and #2. This one genuinely varies by city, so always check.
detergent-bottle: HDPE (#2), one of the most reliably recycled plastics going. And rinsing one takes about three seconds.
cereal-box: The box is recyclable paperboard, but the "waxy" liner inside is plastic film. Box yes, bag no.
wine-bottle: The punt — that dimple in the bottom — makes the bottle stronger and easier to hold while pouring. Form following function since forever.
soup-can: Steel cans are magnetic, so sorters grab them off the belt with giant magnets. The most dramatic rescue on the line.
grocery-bag: Bags jam sorting machinery so often that curbside programs reject them — but grocery store drop-off bins take them back.
plant-pot: Nursery pots are usually #5 plastic, but their shape lets them fall through sorting screens. Technically recyclable, practically rejected.
egg-carton: Paper cartons are made from already-recycled paper and can go around again. Foam ones can't — one more reason to buy the papery kind.
coffee-bag: Multi-layer film: plastic, foil, and paper fused for freshness. Great for beans, impossible to separate.
clamshell: Often the same PET as bottles, but the 3D shape confuses optical sorters. Flat reads fine; clamshells get misread.
black-tray: Near-infrared sorters literally cannot see black plastic, so it gets ejected as trash no matter how clean it is.
film-wrap: Film wraps around sorting screens and shuts down the line. It's the number-one contaminant MRF workers complain about.
razor: Metal, rubber, and plastic fused into one tiny handle. Separating them costs more than the razor, so here it lands.
straw: Too small and light for sorting equipment. Straws fall through the cracks and contaminate the glass stream.
candy-wrapper: The shine is real vaporized aluminum, but far too thin to ever recover. Metallized film, straight to landfill.
headphones: "Tanglers" wrap around sorting screens and stop the whole line for cutting. Workers call them the bane of the MRF.
wet-newspaper: Once paper fibers get soaked they mat together permanently. Wet paper is done, even if it was pristine an hour ago.
acorn: One oak can drop 10,000 acorns in a mast year, and squirrels forget where they buried most of them. Oaks plant themselves by forgetfulness.
pumpkin-guts: The stringy guts are the fruit's placenta — the seeds' life-support system. Compost loves them; your trash bag doesn't need them.
pumpkin-pie: Leftover pie composts, tin and all — well, not the tin. The tin recycles, the pie composts. Teamwork.
mini-gourd: Ornamental gourds are just inedible squash. They'll outlast your Halloween decorations by months in a landfill, or weeks in compost.
candy-wrappers: Americans buy around 600 million pounds of Halloween candy, and nearly every wrapper is metallized film headed for landfill.
halloween-mask: Cheap costume masks are PVC, which can't be recycled and releases nasty chemicals if burned. Landfill is the least-bad option.
cider-jug: Glass recycles forever, but sticky residue can contaminate a whole batch of paper. Hence the rinse.
mini-gourd-1: A rotten gourd is basically pre-composted. Nature did the hard part; the pile just finishes the job.
halloween-mask-1: The average Halloween costume is worn about 7 hours total, and most are plastic that will outlive everyone at the party.
fake-web: Fake webs are spun plastic that tangles exactly like the real thing — in sorting machinery, which is much less charming than your porch.
aluminum-pie-tin: Recycling aluminum takes about 5% of the energy of making it new, and it never degrades. Rinse it and it's practically precious metal.
cracked-bucket: That cracked plastic pumpkin worked one Halloween and will spend 400 years in a landfill. Short career, long retirement.
broken-rake: Garden tools fuse wood, metal, and plastic into one object, which is why even sturdy ones rarely get a second life.
turkey-bone: Bones never recycle, but they do compost — slowly. Months, not weeks. Composters say the marrow makes it worth the wait.
dead-mums: Mums are among America's best-selling potted plants, and most get tossed in black nursery pots — the flower composts, the pot hides from sorters.
growler: Growlers exist because draft beer goes flat in hours. The reusable jug was the original crowler, and Portland takes beer packaging personally.
umbrella: Portland sees rain roughly 150 days a year, making broken umbrellas practically a local species. None of them recycle.
rain-boot: Boot rubber is vulcanized — chemically cross-linked for toughness, which also makes it nearly impossible to recycle.
coffee-cup: Cups are lined with a whisper of plastic to hold hot liquid. That lining is why billions of cups a year can't be recycled.
voodoo-box: That pink box held a doughnut famous enough to draw lines around the block. The grease soaked in means it composts instead of recycling.
pla-container: PLA looks exactly like plastic but it's made from corn starch. An industrial composter breaks it down in months; a landfill just gets confused.
wet-news: Portland rain doesn't dampen newspaper so much as felt it. Once the fibers mat together wet, no sorter can tease them apart.
pack-rings: The six-pack ring was invented in 1960, and the snip-every-ring advice dates to the 80s. Still the simplest wildlife rescue you can do at home.
bike-tube: Butyl rubber tubes are patchable almost forever, which is why Portland bike shops have buckets of them awaiting a second life that rarely comes curbside.
aluminum-foil: A flat sheet of foil falls straight through the sorting screens — but scrunch it into a tight ball and it rides the line like a marble. Golf-ball size is the rule of thumb: if it holds its shape, it counts.
paper-clips: A paper clip is perfectly good steel in a body too small for any sorter to catch. It slips through the screens before the magnets ever see it — right metal, wrong size.
pine-needles: Pine needles are acidic and waxy, so they compost slowly — but they make excellent mulch. Your garden beds won't mind the wait.
holiday-card: Plain paper cards recycle fine. Glitter, foil, and photo paper don't — if it sparkles, it's landfill.
chestnut-shells: Roasted chestnuts are a winter tradition, and their shells are pure compost. The song lied though — nobody's roasting them on an open fire anymore.
wrap-tube: The cardboard tube inside wrapping paper is just a paper towel tube in a fancy coat. Recycle it like one.
gift-wrap: Most gift wrap can't be recycled — the foil and plastic coatings contaminate the paper stream. The scrunch test never lies: if it stays crumpled, it's recyclable.
ribbon: Ribbon tangles in sorting machinery like Christmas lights in a box. Cut it up or bin it — never recycle it loose.
orange-peels: Winter citrus peaks when nothing else is fresh. The peels are compost gold — and they make your bin smell like a grove instead of garbage.
dead-poinsettia: That poinsettia was doomed the day it left the greenhouse. Compost it guilt-free — they're bred for December, not longevity.
fruitcake: The average fruitcake is 60% dried fruit and 40% regret. Compost handles both. Some fruitcakes are allegedly older than the people re-gifting them.
cookie-tin: A tin is steel, and steel recycles forever without losing quality. That popcorn tin from 2019 has probably been five different cans by now.
advent-calendar: Cardboard, foil, plastic trays, and chocolate dust — an advent calendar is four materials in a trench coat. Landfill it and move on.
broken-ornament: Broken glass ornaments can't go in glass recycling — they're a different glass formula and a hazard to sorters. Wrap the shards before binning.
string-lights: A tangled string of lights can shut down a sorting line for an hour. They're e-waste, not landfill — but they never belong in the bin.
tinsel: Tinsel is plastic film with delusions of grandeur. It wraps around sorting discs like seaweed on a propeller — straight to landfill.
ice-scraper: A plastic ice scraper is too rigid and mixed to recycle curbside. Use it until it snaps, then landfill the pieces.
watermelon-rind: Watermelon rind is 95% water and composts fast — pickled rind is also a real Southern delicacy. Your compost pile won't judge either way.
corn-cob: A corn cob is basically a sponge made of plant fiber. Compost it, or do what your grandparents did and use it as a scrub brush.
peach-pit: Peach pits are so hard they can survive composting intact — smash them first or they'll outlast everything else in the pile.
broken-flip-flop: Flip-flops are foam, rubber, and plastic straps fused together — three materials, zero recyclability. A billion pairs are sold every year.
popped-beach-ball: A beach ball is PVC film: technically plastic, practically unrecyclable. Patch it if you can — a popped ball is a landfill ball.
crab-shell: Crab shells are chitin, the same stuff in insect exoskeletons. Compost loves them, and they add calcium too. The feast continues underground.
bug-spray-can: Aerosol cans stay pressurized even when they feel empty — that leftover propellant is a hazard at the sorting line. Landfill keeps everyone safe.
snow-cone-cup: That waxy coating that keeps your snow cone from soaking through is exactly what keeps it out of the paper recycling stream.
coconut-shell: Coconut shells are so tough they're turned into charcoal, bowls, and buttons. In a compost pile they're slow but steady — nature's Tupperware.
cracked-frisbee: A frisbee is HDPE, the same plastic as milk jugs — but its shape and mixed dyes make it unrecyclable curbside. Throw it, don't bin it.
broken-straw-hat: A straw hat is just woven grass — pure compost. It shaded you all summer; let it feed the soil next.
grass-clippings: Grass clippings are nitrogen-rich and compost in days. Leave them on the lawn and they feed it directly — the original closed loop.
potting-soil: The soil inside is fine for the ground — it's the plastic bag that isn't. Empty it, then landfill the bag.
dead-seedlings: Most seedlings die from love — overwatering. Compost the failures and start again; every gardener has a graveyard.
veggie-scraps: Veggie scraps are the backbone of home compost. Chop them small and they'll vanish in weeks.
nursery-pot: Those flimsy black nursery pots are polypropylene — recyclable, but only if rinsed. Soil contaminates the plastic stream.
floral-foam: Floral foam looks like a sponge but it's phenolic plastic — it crumbles into microplastics and never breaks down. Landfill, always.
chipped-terracotta: Terracotta is fired clay — basically a brick. It can't be melted down or pulped, so cracked pots go to landfill, not the recycle bin.
plastic-eggs: Those snap-apart Easter eggs are polystyrene — too small and mixed to recycle. They'll outlive the candy they held by about 400 years.
bubble-bottle: A sticky bubble bottle needs a rinse before recycling — sugar residue contaminates the plastic stream just like food does.
garden-hose: A garden hose is PVC wrapped around fabric — two materials that can't be separated. Landfill it when it finally springs a leak.
broken-kite: A broken kite is ripstop nylon on fiberglass spars — light, tangly, and unrecyclable. A good gust is its natural end.
daffodil-stems: Daffodil stems contain toxic alkaloids — it's why deer won't touch them. Compost handles the toxins fine; the deer stay away on their own.
seed-packet: Seed packets list a germination rate, usually 70-90%. The rest is optimism. Expired seeds still make fine compost.
plant-tag: Plant tags are tiny polystyrene — too small for sorters to catch. Keep them for your garden journal or bin them.
broken-trowel: A trowel fuses steel to a plastic or wood handle — when the handle snaps, the whole tool is landfill. Buy one with a lifetime warranty.
popsicle-stick: Popsicle sticks are birchwood and compost in weeks. The flavor stains are just proof of a good summer.
sunscreen-bottle: Sunscreen bottles are HDPE — rinse and recycle. Leftover lotion contaminates the plastic stream just like food residue.
solo-cup: Solo cups are polystyrene — technically plastic, practically unrecyclable. Billions get used at parties every single year.
pool-noodle: Pool noodles are polyethylene foam — same family as plastic bags, but too bulky and low-value to recycle curbside.
dirty-tea-bags: Tea leaves are nitrogen-rich compost gold. The paper bag breaks down right along with them.
dirty-toilet-paper-roll: A clean cardboard tube is recyclable. Once it's soiled, it contaminates the paper batch.
dirty-toothbrush: The average toothbrush takes 400+ years to break down. Bamboo handles are the compostable alternative.
dirty-plastic-fork: Single-use cutlery is the wrong shape and usually the wrong plastic. It jams the sorting line.
